title: The Story of Saint Veronica Giuliani
summary: From a little girl in Mercatello to fifty years of prayer and practical love in one monastery - the story of Veronica, the "true image."
coverAlt: Illustration from the Saint Veronica Giuliani storybook: newborn Orsola in her mother's arms in a modest stone home in Mercatello, 1660, her father and young sisters gathered around

pages.title: Mercatello, 1660
pages.body: In the year 1660, in Mercatello, a little town in a green valley in Italy, a baby girl was born. Her parents, Francesco and Benedetta, named her Orsola. She was the youngest of seven sisters. Three of those sisters would also become nuns. Nobody could have guessed, that day, what this youngest sister would become. But God had a plan for her. And years later, Orsola would receive a new name: Veronica. It means "true image."

pages.title: A Wish Grows in Piacenza
pages.body: When Orsola was seven years old, her mother died. Her father found new work in a city called Piacenza, and the family moved there with him. An old story says that even as a little girl, Orsola shared her food with poor children. And in Piacenza, she began to feel something growing in her heart: a wish to give her whole life to Jesus.

pages.title: Her Father's Other Plans
pages.body: A wish like that can be hard to follow. Orsola's father had other plans for her. He wanted her to marry, and he found young men who hoped to be her husband. But Orsola's heart was set on a different home: a convent, where sisters live simply and pray together. She waited. She hoped. And at last, her father said yes.

pages.title: A New Name
pages.body: In 1677, when Orsola was seventeen, she walked through the door of a monastery in Città di Castello. A monastery is a place where sisters pray, work, and live close to God. Orsola was now a Capuchin Poor Clare sister, and she was given her new name: Veronica. She would stay in that one monastery for fifty years.

pages.title: She Stayed
pages.body: The first years were not easy. Sometimes Veronica was tempted to give it all up and go back to the world outside. She stayed. One year later, in 1678, she stood in front of her sisters and made her solemn promises: her whole life, given to God. She meant to keep it.

pages.title: The Teacher Who Prayed
pages.body: Veronica did not only pray. For thirty-four years, she was the sister who taught the new sisters. She guided them wisely and carefully. She would not even let them read mystical books. She also wrote many letters and poems. And she prayed for people she would never meet: for the Pope, for priests, for everyone in need. "To suffer with joy," she wrote, "is the key to love." Little by little, the people guiding her saw that her prayer was something out of the ordinary.

pages.title: Twenty-Two Thousand Pages
pages.body: So in 1693, a priest and her bishop told Veronica to write it all down: her whole life with God. She obeyed. Day after day, year after year, she wrote for thirty-four years, about 22,000 pages, all by hand, with no crossings-out. We call it her Diary. In it, she wrote about her prayer, and about how close she felt to Jesus. The Church's old records also say that, in a way no one can fully explain, she shared in his suffering. But Veronica never wrote about pain to be proud of it. She wrote about love.

pages.title: The Abbess and the Water Pipes
pages.body: Years passed. In 1716, the sisters chose her as their abbess, the leader of the monastery. The sisters would keep on choosing her for the rest of her life. She used her new job for everyday things. The monastery had never had a proper water supply, so she had pipes laid to bring the water in. She had the convent made bigger, too. For Veronica, love was not only something you feel. It is something you build.

pages.title: I Have Found Love
pages.body: Veronica grew very sick. After a long illness, she died on July 9, 1727. She was sixty-six years old. Her last words were: "I have found Love, Love has let himself be seen! ... Tell everyone about it, tell everyone!" In 1839, the Church declared her a saint. Her feast day is July 9, the day she went home to God. Orsola had become Veronica: a true image of the love she had followed all her life.

pages.title: Points of Reflection
pages.body: What do you think was hardest for Veronica? Waiting to enter the monastery? Staying when it was hard? Or praying for people she had never met? With a grown-up, read Romans chapter 8, verses 38 and 39. In this book's words: nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God. Today, quietly pray for one person who is sad or far away. And if you ever feel sad yourself, tell a trusted grown-up. God, thank you for loving us. Help us to love others the way Veronica did. Saint Veronica, pray for us. Amen.
